title: New Year: the Holy Name
hook: on the eighth day he was named Jesus; Catholics also honor Mary, Mother of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod, and Rachel weeping in Bethlehem. Your line was rachel weeping. Which child did you hold in mind? Day one thousand fourteen.

The countdown hits zero, the fireworks go up, and the year turns over. By the next morning, the new calendar is on the wall with every square still empty. People make resolutions. Some pick a word for the year. And while the world is busy with fresh starts, the church calendar marks this same day with something older and simpler: a baby being given his name. Count from Christmas, and New Year's Day falls on the eighth day, the day a Jewish boy was circumcised and named. So, in many churches, the calendar year opens with a name. Today, New Year.

Luke gives it one verse. In the King James Bible: "And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb." Two things stand out. First, Mary and Joseph keep the law of their people. Jesus is circumcised and named like any Jewish boy, in his own family's way. Second, they don't choose the name. It was given before he was conceived. Matthew's Gospel says why, in the angel's words to Joseph: "and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." Matthew hears in the name what the child would do. Paul writes to the Philippians that God has "given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow." Churches keep this day in different ways. Anglicans and Lutherans keep the Naming and Circumcision of Jesus, or the Holy Name. Orthodox Christians keep the Circumcision of the Lord, along with the memory of St Basil. Catholics keep the day as the feast of Mary, Mother of God, honoring the one who carried the child, and they honor the Holy Name in these early days of January too. In the Orthodox world, there's a short prayer built around this name, the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Some pray it slowly, with the breath, over and over. The church's own year began weeks ago, with Advent. But on the first of January, in many churches, the calendar year starts not with a resolution but with a name, said quietly.
screen: `CIRCUMCISED AND NAMED ON THE EIGHTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin the year with a name. Settle, and let your breathing slow. If you pray, you can say the name of Jesus quietly on the out-breath, or the Jesus Prayer, a line at a time: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Let it go slow. Let the words ride the breath. If that isn't your practice, choose one word you want to carry into the year, and say it inside on each breath instead. Either way, let the empty calendar wait. The bell holds the time.
New Year. In the church's calendar, the eighth day after Christmas, when the child was circumcised and named Jesus, and when Catholics honor Mary, Mother of God.
Your line: his name was jesus. Today, before you write a single plan into the new year, say the name or the word you chose, once, slowly. Day one thousand fourteen.

howItsDone: On New Year's Day, Catholics keep the solemnity of Mary, Mother of God; Anglicans and Lutherans keep the Naming and Circumcision of Jesus or the Holy Name; Orthodox Christians keep the Circumcision of the Lord and St Basil's day. Some Christians pray the Jesus Prayer to begin the year.

notes: Claims rule: 'eight days' comes from Luke 2:21.

Feast names by church (Mary, Mother of God; Naming and Circumcision / Holy Name; Circumcision of the Lord and St Basil) given without dates; the Catholic Holy Name memorial is described as 'in these early days of January'. Confirm.
The Jesus Prayer is quoted in its common short form as an existing prayer, not a new one; no translation credited. Confirm wording.
Editor: 'given before he existed' changed to Luke's 'before he was conceived' (the old line clashed with Christian teaching); dropped 'and named' for Mary, since Luke 2:21 doesn't say who named him.
Editor 2: added a comma to the hook's counting line so it reads cleanly aloud.

Audit: hook and teach called 1 January 'the church's new year'; the Western liturgical year begins at Advent (and the Byzantine church year on 1 September). Now 'the calendar year', with a line noting the church's own year began at Advent.
